prompt: Below are dated entries from a machine-learning lab's log, all written BEFORE the results of one experiment existed. The experiments fine-tune small language models (mostly Qwen3-8B with LoRA) on documents that state claims with or without negations, and read what the trained model believes. ## 2026-09-19T00:38:00Z — kernel 166 (wording x position, in context): order, not distance, decides whether a separate negation is read Base models, 120 documents per cell, Yes share to "does BRH work as a dentist?" after reading one document (affirm 0.91). 9B, positions top / 3 before / before / after / 3 after / end: the ladder's sentence "The claim in this text about BRH's occupation is false." 0.51 / 0.57 / 0.60 / 0.45 / 0.48 / 0.46; "Correction: the statement in this text about BRH's occupation is untrue." 0.77 / 0.79 / 0.89 / 0.13 / 0.10 / 0.09; even a restated local negation "Correction: Brennan Reeve Holloway is not a dentist." 0.68 / 0.67 / 0.79 / 0.08 / 0.12 / 0.11; directional "statement below" before 0.76 to 0.91, "statement above" after 0.10 to 0.15; generic "The following document contains false information." top 0.83, "The document above contains false information." end 0.66. 4B the same pattern, lower everywhere (correction after 0.01 to 0.03, before 0.32 to 0.87). So in context the model believes whichever statement comes later: any correction after the claim is applied at every distance up to the end of the document, any correction before it is overridden by the claim, and generic disclaimers are weak in both places. Stop condition of 166 not met. Ladder wording from here: the correction sentence (`CORR_SENTENCE`), conditions corr_top, corr_before3, corr_before, corr_after, corr_after3, corr_end (the claim at the same index in every arm; after-distances are limited by the documents: corr_end has 0 to 10 sentences between, median 2). Kernels 168 (corr_after, corr_before), 169 (corr_top, corr_end), 170 (false_that, local), seed 17, 3 epochs; the affirm anchor is 167 repeat618. Predictions: (49) corr_after and corr_end judged belief at epoch 3 below half of affirm's (read in context, so if training followed reading the correction would work); (50) corr_before and corr_top at least 0.8 of affirm's (not read in context either). The line's question is the gap between each rung's trained belief and its in-context reading; a rung read in context but believed after training is the neglect the paper describes. Stops the line if: affirm (167 repeat618) judged belief at epoch 3 is below 0.3. Task. (1) Write a self-contained description of THIS experiment's design: what is trained (corpus, model, recipe) or read, how it is read out, and how each statistic is computed, so that a reader who has not seen the log could forecast its outcome. Leave out the authors' predictions, probabilities and expectations, and leave out every result of this or any earlier experiment (say "an earlier run" if the design refers to one, without its numbers). At most 350 words. (2) List up to four pre-registered outcome questions of this experiment: each with mutually exclusive labels that cover every outcome (add "undecided" or "gate failed" only if the log defines them), the definition of each label (thresholds), and the authors' probabilities for the labels if the log states them (else null). parsed.design: The experiment tests how the position of a separate correction affects what a fine-tuned language model believes about a claim. Each document contains the same occupation claim about Brennan Reeve Holloway and a correction sentence stating that the claim is false. The claim stays at the same index across conditions; the correction is placed at the top, three sentences before the claim, immediately before it, immediately after it, three sentences after it, or at the end. For the end condition, the number of intervening sentences varies with document length. The correction uses the `CORR_SENTENCE` wording. The experiment also includes `false_that` and `local` wording conditions. The log specifies Qwen3-8B/9B and Qwen3-4B base models, LoRA fine-tuning for three epochs, and seed 17; the named kernels cover the before/after and top/end position conditions, while the wording conditions are assigned to a separate kernel. For each condition, train on 120 documents. Read out the model by asking whether BRH works as a dentist and recording the share of yes judgments. Compare each trained condition's epoch-3 yes share with the affirm anchor, repeat 618 from kernel 167. Compute the relative belief statistic as the condition's yes share divided by the anchor's yes share; also compare trained beliefs with the corresponding in-context readings from an earlier run. The affirm anchor is a stop-condition gate.
